lecons.html:
Why this module?

A citizen who knows his rights without knowing his limits sooner or later ends up before a judge. A citizen who knows his limits without knowing his rights ends up letting himself be pushed around. This module gives you both.

“Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God.” (Rom 13:1)

In its context, this text first targets political authorities. It calls us to respect the institutions and laws of the nation where we live, as long as they do not oppose the Word of God. Here is the full passage:

“Let every soul be in subjection to the higher authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those who exist are ordained by God. Therefore he who resists the authority withstands the ordinance of God; and those who withstand will receive to themselves judgment. For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil. Do you desire to have no fear of the authority? Do that which is good, and you will have praise from the authority, for he is a servant of God to you for good. But if you do that which is evil, be afraid, for he doesn’t bear the sword in vain; for he is a servant of God, an avenger for wrath to him who does evil. Therefore you need to be in subjection, not only because of the wrath, but also for conscience’ sake. For this reason you also pay taxes, for they are servants of God’s service, continually doing this very thing. Therefore give everyone what you owe: if you owe taxes, pay taxes; if customs, then customs; if respect, then respect; if honor, then honor.” (Rom 13:1-7)

Obeying authorities does not mean keeping silent with your head down. It means knowing the law, respecting it by conviction, and also knowing how to have it respected when it is you it protects.

When people live together, rules are needed so that the stronger does not crush the weaker. On the road, it is the one in the most hurry who would like to crush the slower. At work, it is the boss who could crush the employee, or the employee who could cheat the boss. At home, it is the adult who could crush the child. The law is a protection: it protects everyone, including you.

What must change in your life

  • You know your fundamental rights, and you know where to read them.
  • You know what the law allows and forbids to someone who preaches, teaches or leads an assembly.
  • You know the common offenses on social networks, and you no longer commit them.
  • You know how to organize a place of worship in compliance with the noise regulation.
  • You know the basic rules of the road, of work, of the family and of the child.
  • You know how to react when facing an authority: identity check, search, arrest, a neighbor’s complaint.
  • You respect the law by conviction, not out of fear.

The method

We are not going to copy out articles of law: you would remember nothing. For each text, we explain what it says, with the reference so that you can go and read it yourself. Reading the law in its official source is the difference between someone who has heard about the law and someone who holds it in his hands. Be one of those who hold it.

Read this first. The articles, amounts and procedures cited in this module are those of the texts at the time of writing. Texts change: an article number or an amount may have changed since. What does not change is the essential: what the law targets, what it protects and what it forbids, as we say it here. Before relying on an article, always check the version in force. This module informs you, it does not replace a professional: if you have a real problem, turn to a lawyer, a bailiff, the labor inspectorate or the social service of your municipality.

PartThe textWhat touches your life
1The Constitution and the African CharterYour rights and duties as a citizen
2The Penal CodePreaching, teaching, leading
3The Digital CodeYour phone, Facebook, WhatsApp
4The decree on noiseYour place of worship and your neighbors
5The Highway CodeThe road, the motorbike, the helmet
6The Labor CodeYour job, your employees
7The Code of Persons and the FamilyMarriage, children, inheritance
8The Child CodeDiscipline, school, placed children
9Real situationsHow to react when facing an authority

The Constitution of Benin guarantees specific rights to every citizen. These are not favors: they are rights. Here is what it says in the articles below. These references are those of the text at the time of writing: texts change, check the version in force (National Assembly, General Secretariat of the Government, town hall).

What the Constitution guarantees

ArticleThe rightWhat this means for you
Art. 23Freedom of thought, conscience, religion and worshipYou can choose your faith, practice it and express it, with respect for public order and the secularism of the State. Religious communities develop freely and manage their affairs autonomously.
Art. 15 to 19Freedom, presumption of innocence, prohibition of tortureYou are innocent until your guilt is established, with all the guarantees of defense (art. 17). No one may be tortured or mistreated (art. 18). No agent of the State is bound to obey an order that seriously violates human rights (art. 19).
Art. 18Length of police custodyNo one may be held more than 48 hours without the decision of a magistrate. This length may be extended only in exceptional cases provided for by law, and never beyond eight days. You may ask to be examined by a doctor of your choice.
Art. 20Inviolability of the homeNo one may enter your home or search your house outside the forms and conditions provided for by law.
Art. 21 and 22Secrecy of communications; right of propertyYour letters, calls and messages are protected by law. Your property may be taken from you only for reasons of public utility, with fair compensation.
Art. 25Freedom to come and go, of association, assembly, procession and demonstrationThe State guarantees these freedoms under the conditions set by law. Your assembly, your association can meet and act legally.
Art. 26Equality before the lawNo distinction of origin, race, sex, religion, opinion or social situation. The State protects the family, particularly the mother and the child.

Two points deserve emphasis. First, any citizen can refer a matter to the Constitutional Court to challenge a law or an act that violates his rights (art. 3 and 122). Second, the Constitution specifies (art. 7) that the rights proclaimed by the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, ratified by Benin on January 20, 1986, are part of Beninese law.

What the African Charter guarantees

ArticleThe right protectedWhy it concerns you
Art. 2Enjoying one’s rights without discrimination, notably of religion or opinionYour faith cannot be a ground for discrimination.
Art. 6Liberty and security: no one may be arbitrarily arrestedEvery arrest must rest on a legal basis.
Art. 7The right to have one’s case heard: defense, impartial judgeYou have the right to a defense and to a fair trial.
Art. 8Freedom of conscience, profession and free practice of religionProtected at the African level, not only the Beninese.
Art. 10 and 11Freedoms of association and assemblyYour assemblies are protected.

Your duties as a citizen

Rights and duties are inseparable. An exemplary Christian is the first to fulfill his civic duties, not out of fear of the law, but because it is right.

ArticleThe duty
Constitution, art. 33Working for the common good, fulfilling one’s civic and professional obligations, and paying one’s taxes. A Christian who cheats the tax authorities violates the law and bears a poor witness.
Constitution, art. 34Respecting, in all circumstances, the Constitution, the constitutional order, the laws and regulations of the Republic.
Constitution, art. 36Respecting and regarding one’s fellow man without discrimination, and maintaining relations of dialogue, tolerance and peace. This is the law of love of neighbor, put into action.
Constitution, art. 37Respecting and protecting public property: roads, schools, hospitals. Damaging them is stealing from the community.
African Charter, art. 29Supporting one’s family and serving one’s national community.

To think about

  • Someone tries to ban a prayer meeting in your neighborhood. What do you rely on, calmly?
  • An officer has held you for three days without charge. Which article do you invoke?
  • An officer shows up at your home to search the house. What questions do you ask him before opening?
  • What steps are needed to legally register a religious association?

lecons.titre: The Penal Code and those who speak
lecons.html:
Why a part that addresses those who preach? Because someone who speaks from a pulpit, a microphone or a platform is not in the same situation as someone chatting at the market. Those who listen to him trust him, and some verify nothing. If a leader tells his assembly that such and such a civil servant is a thief, many will believe it without looking further. The law takes this authority into account. It does not stop you from speaking. It simply says that the more influence you have, the more responsible you are for what you do with it.

The Penal Code devotes several articles to what the law says to those who exercise a ministry: these are articles 387 to 393. We look at three: 388, 389 and 391. For each: what it targets, what you risk, and how not to fall into it. Then go and read them yourself in the official text.

1. Article 388: contempt and defamation of a public official

Contempt is insult, displayed scorn. Defamation is publicly accusing someone of a specific act that damages his honor. If it touches an agent of the State (a police officer, a mayor, a service director, a magistrate) and it is said from the pulpit, you expose yourself to a fine of 200,000 to 1,000,000 CFA francs and/or imprisonment of one month to one year.

What is the difference between criticizing a public policy and defaming a public official? Compare these two sentences:

  • “The waste management in our municipality does not meet the needs of the inhabitants, and we must pray and act so that it changes.” Here, we are talking about a situation and a decision.
  • “Mr. So-and-so, of the technical department, stole the municipality’s money.” Here, a person is accused, by name, of a specific act. Without established proof, this is exactly what the law wants to punish.

Even if you think you are right, the pulpit is not a courtroom. There are provided channels: a letter, a complaint, a lawyer. The pulpit is for teaching, exhorting and praying. It is not for settling scores.

2. Article 389: provocation to resist the laws

Pushing worshipers to resist the law, or setting citizens against one another, from a place of worship, is an offense: three months to two years of imprisonment. Does this mean one can no longer speak of justice or injustice? No. Here is where the line runs.

What you can doWhat you cannot do
Teach what the Bible says about justice, honesty, care for the poor, the widow and the orphan.Tell your assembly not to obey such and such a law.
Pray for your leaders, as 1 Timothy 2:1-2 asks.Refuse to pay a certain tax, or call for refusing it.
Encourage your worshipers to vote, to inform themselves, to go through legal channels: letter to the town hall, association, petition, lawyer.Oppose the officers, or set one part of the citizens against another.

Some think of Acts 5:29: “We must obey God rather than men.” Look at what the apostles do in this chapter. They themselves answer before the Sanhedrin, and they themselves accept the blows (Acts 5:40-41). They do not rouse the crowd against the authorities. When your personal conscience puts you in real conflict with a law, you bear the responsibility yourself. You do not drag a whole assembly with you.

3. Article 391: writings count as much as words

The same logic applies to what you write. Any published writing that pushes people to disobey the laws is punished by two to five years of imprisonment. This covers books and tracts, but also Facebook posts and WhatsApp messages. What you write on your phone has the same weight as what you say aloud before the assembly, with one difference: writing remains, it is copied, it circulates, and you no longer control it.

The offenses of public defamation and insult are also provided for by the Code of Information and Communication (Law No. 2015-07 of March 20, 2015), which applies to the press and, as we will see, to what is published online.

Four questions before publishing

  1. Am I calling someone to disobey a law?
  2. Am I naming a person, and do I have what it takes to prove it?
  3. Would I dare say exactly the same thing to this person, to their face, in front of a witness?
  4. Does this build something, or does it mainly relieve me?

If even one of these answers bothers you, do not publish tonight. Sleep on it, and reread your text tomorrow.

The text is called Law No. 2017-20 of April 20, 2018 establishing the Digital Code in the Republic of Benin. Of all the laws in this module, it is the one you are most likely to run into. It does not concern only journalists or well-known people. It concerns anyone who has a phone and a Facebook or WhatsApp account, including from his personal phone, at home, on a Sunday evening.

Journalists, bloggers and ordinary citizens have been prosecuted on this basis. The OCRC (Central Office for the Repression of Cybercrime) investigates and makes arrests. Trials are held before the CRIET (Court for the Repression of Economic Offenses and Terrorism). Remember these two acronyms: the day you hear about a summons to the OCRC, you will know what it is about.

An example. In December 2019, the journalist Ignace Sossou was arrested after relaying on social networks remarks made by a public prosecutor. He was convicted of “harassment through electronic communications”, with a prison sentence reduced on appeal to twelve months, six of them to be served. We do not cite this case to judge the court’s decision, but to show what the mere fact of relaying can cost.

This law is debated: organizations ask for the revision of article 550, which they consider too broad. But as long as a text is in force, it applies. When you go and read Book VI of the Code, check which version is in force.

Watch out for numbers. The Digital Code and the Penal Code both have an “article 550”, an “article 551”, etc. These are different texts. In this part, we mean the Digital Code.

Article 550: harassment and false information

This article is one of the most used to prosecute Beninese. It targets two behaviors that must be kept separate.

  • Harassment by electronic communication: initiating a communication that coerces, intimidates, harasses or causes emotional distress to a person.
  • False information: initiating or relaying false information against a person, through social networks or any other electronic medium.

Notice the word “relays”. It does not only target the one who invents: it also targets the one who forwards. Here is a situation. A friend sends you information about a politician. You share it in your WhatsApp group. It is false. Are you concerned? Yes, you can be. Saying “it is my friend who sent it to me” does not automatically protect you: it is the judge who assesses, but you will already have had the summons, perhaps the police custody, and the lawyer to pay.

The practical rule: before forwarding, verify. Who is the source? Is this information found in a serious media outlet? If you cannot verify, do not share. This applies especially to those messages that say “share before it gets deleted”: that is precisely the kind of message you must not relay.

Article 551: racist or religious insult

It targets whoever deliberately insults a person, by electronic means, because of his race, religion, origin or opinions. The penalty can range from six months to seven years of prison, with a fine of one to ten million CFA francs.

Why dwell on it? Because, in the Christian milieu, the temptation exists to make fun of other religions: Islam, indigenous religions, another church. A funny video passed between friends. A mocking comment on Facebook, even as a joke, can fall under this article. The text speaks of a deliberate insult, but the one who jokes does not decide how the judge, or the targeted person, will read his joke. And the proof is your post, with your name on it.

One can disagree with a doctrine. One can explain why one believes something else. The apostle Peter asks us to give an account of our hope “with humility and fear” (1 Pet 3:15). What the law forbids is lowering a person because of his faith.

Articles 552 and 553: incitement to hatred, violence, rebellion

Article 552 punishes incitement to hatred and violence against a person or a group: up to one year in prison and five million francs in fines, or either of these two penalties. Article 553 punishes direct provocation to rebellion through an electronic communication network: from six months in prison and two to ten million francs in fines.

Example: a preacher publishes a message calling his worshipers to reject another religious community. The logic is the same as for article 389 of the Penal Code, seen above: what is targeted is the call to rise up against someone or against a group. And a message sent to thousands of people cannot be taken back.

Article 558: the online press

Defamation, public insult, apology for crime: when committed by electronic means, they are punished by the same penalties as in the traditional press (2015 law on the Code of Information and Communication). In other words, what you publish online is judged like what a newspaper publishes on paper. This applies to a Facebook page, a blog, a YouTube channel. A closed WhatsApp group does not put you out of reach: messages can be captured, forwarded and used as proof.

Criticizing is discussing an act, with facts, in a proper tone. Example: “This decision closed three schools in our neighborhood, and here are the figures.” Defaming is accusing someone of a specific act, without proof, to harm his reputation. Insulting is hurling words at him that lower him. A criticism that rests on facts is easily defended before a judge. A criticism that rests on anger is poorly defended.

What Beninese really risk

The offenseThe orders of magnitude
Art. 550: harassment, false informationPrison and fine. Depending on the case, up to two years in prison and up to ten million francs in fines.
Art. 551: racist or religious insultSix months to seven years in prison, one to ten million francs in fines.
Art. 552: incitement to hatred and violenceUp to one year in prison and five million francs in fines, or either.
Art. 553: provocation to rebellionAt least six months in prison, two to ten million francs in fines.
Art. 558: online pressThe penalties of the Code of Information and Communication.

These are not symbolic fines. Always check the amounts in the text in force.

The seven golden rules for not going to prison because of your phone

  1. Never relay information without verifying it. Sharing is being responsible.
  2. Never insult, humiliate or threaten someone online. Even in private, even in a closed group: the digital proof remains.
  3. Never publish content that calls for the rejection of a religion, an ethnic group or a group. Even in the form of a joke.
  4. Do not criticize a public official by name in an insulting way. Criticizing a decision is allowed, attacking a person is forbidden.
  5. Keep a copy of your important posts. In case of dispute, the proof of your good faith and of the exact context can save you.
  6. In case of arrest, ask for a lawyer right away, and sign nothing before you have read and understood what is written.
  7. Download and read Book VI of the Digital Code. It is the complete reference.

This is Decree No. 2022-301 of May 25, 2022 regulating noise in the Republic of Benin. It replaces a text from 2001. Some think noise is a minor subject next to prison. That is not the case. Noise nuisances are among the most frequent environmental offenses, and the text expressly cites places of worship among the sources of noise. Cases have been reported where music equipment was seized in the middle of a service. This is not theoretical.

The five rules to know

The ruleWhat it says, and what it changes for your assembly
1. The hoursIn residential areas, noisy activities and events, including in places of worship, are forbidden on working days from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. and from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., and on rest days from 8 p.m. to 10 a.m. A prayer vigil with sound equipment after 10 p.m. on a working day is forbidden. A Sunday service that starts at 7 a.m. with drums and amplifiers, audible outside, as well. The text targets the noise that goes out from your place, not the fact of gathering to pray.
2. Sound levelsOutside these time slots, there are also limits in decibels. The Departmental Directorate of the Living Environment indicates about 60 decibels outdoors in a residential area. In soundproofed buildings, the level is limited to 70 decibels: even if your hall is soundproofed, you cannot turn it up just anywhere. The exact table in the decree varies according to zone and time: read it.
3. Loudspeakers and tarp hallsOutdoor sound devices (sirens, loudspeakers, horns) are forbidden, except to report an accident or serious incident. Evangelizing in the street with a loudspeaker is therefore an offense. Party halls under tarps operated professionally are forbidden across the territory.
4. Prior authorizationBefore opening a noise-generating activity, you must obtain, as the case may be, a technical opinion from the Departmental Directorate of the Living Environment or an environmental compliance certificate issued by the Beninese Environment Agency. A leader’s first step is to find out whether his place of worship has this opinion.
5. DistanceNoise sources must be located at least 200 meters from sensitive establishments (hospitals, schools, etc.) according to article 7 of the decree.

The exceptional exemption

For an exceptional event (a convention, a large vigil), the mayor may grant a special exemption for the use of sound devices in public places. It is framed: 80 decibels at most and 48 hours at most. Make the request beforehand, in writing, to the town hall. The authorization specifies the date, place and duration.

Who checks?

The Environmental Police and the territorial units of the Republican Police can record offenses, receive complaints and arrest a person presumed to be the author of noise nuisances. In practice, everything often begins with a neighbor’s complaint. The officers can measure the noise with a device: if you are within the norms, you are protected. If you receive an official summons, do not ignore it. The classic mistake is to negotiate informally without settling the legal situation.

This week, if you lead a place of worship

  • In which zone is your hall located? Is it in a residential area?
  • At what hours do your services, vigils and choir rehearsals take place?
  • Do you have the opinion of the Departmental Directorate of the Living Environment?
  • Is your hall soundproofed? Are the loudspeakers facing inward? At what level do you set the volume?
  • Is an exceptional event planned? Have you made the request to the mayor?

If you do not lead, you still have a role: inform your leader of what you have learned.

One last word on neighbors. Many complaints are born from a neighbor who has had enough and to whom no one has ever spoken. A courteous exchange is worth more than ten explanations before an officer. “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” (Rom 12:18) As much as it depends on you: this is exactly what the decree asks of you.

The road is our first school of civic sense. If you want to know whether a country is civilized, look at its intersections: on the road, no one is watching you all the time. It is your conscience against your haste. In Cotonou, Porto-Novo, Parakou, Abomey-Calavi, you know the reality: motorbikes everywhere, the zémidjans slipping through, trucks driving fast, pedestrians crossing wherever they can. And, unfortunately, accidents. The law exists on this subject so that people go home in the evening.

Where is the Highway Code?

For a long time, traffic rules were scattered across several texts: laws, decrees, orders. The government acknowledged it. On September 24, 2025, it adopted a bill establishing a Highway Code to gather these rules into a single, more readable text, with clearer penalties, and sent it to the National Assembly. At the time of writing this module, we have not found confirmation of its vote: when it is voted and published, find out about the changes. In the meantime, the basic rules below are already applied in the field. Since September 21, 2026, the Republican Police has been carrying out new checks: red lights, helmet, seat belt, phone, traffic lanes and administrative papers.

The helmet: driver and passenger

Wearing a helmet is mandatory for motorcyclists, driver and passenger. Since April 2024, the fixed fine for not wearing a helmet is 5,000 CFA francs (it was 10,000 F). Let us do a little math. 5,000 francs is the price of a good meal. A decent helmet costs a few thousand francs. A head injury costs months in hospital, millions of francs, and sometimes a life.

“But I am just making a short trip.” Many serious accidents happen less than two kilometers from home. The road does not ask about distance. It asks only for a second of inattention.

A dad takes his son to school by motorbike, morning after morning, without a helmet for the child, because “we are in a hurry, it is nearby”. One day, a truck backs up, a car cuts across the road, a slip. The dad gets up with scratches. The little one does not.

This image is not here to frighten. It is here to stay in your memory.

The phone, overloading, wrong way, red light

  • The phone at the wheel or handlebars. At sixty kilometers an hour, you travel sixteen meters per second. Five seconds looking at a screen are eighty meters traveled without seeing, almost the length of a football field.
  • Overloading. Two children, an older brother, a sack of corn, all on one motorbike. It is the reality of many families, but a motorbike is not made for that: it brakes poorly and tips over easily. If you must carry several people, make two trips. It costs time, not blood.
  • Going the wrong way to save three minutes. Those coming the other way are not expecting you, and in case of a crash, it is you who is wrong before the law.
  • The red light, the seat belt, the reserved lanes. They are part of the current checks.

The papers

During a check, you may be asked for your driver’s license, your insurance (the proof that, if you injure someone, a company can pay), the technical inspection (which proves the vehicle is fit to drive), proof of payment of the motor vehicle tax, as well as the license plate. They also look at the lights and tires.

Why is insurance so important? A zémidjan without insurance knocks down a pedestrian. The pedestrian has a broken leg and cannot work for three months. Who pays? If the driver is not insured, it is he, out of his own pocket, or the victim is left with nothing. In many cases, both lose.

The license itself is changing. According to an order of May 26, 2026, the code exam is separated from the practical exam: the candidate must follow at least 60 hours of code classes and 30 hours of practical training, the theory exam takes place on a digital medium, and passing the code is valid for 12 months. The text also opens the way to a points-based license, later. The message is clear: the license is not a paper you “arrange”, it is the proof that you know how to drive.

Fines: paying properly

This point touches our honesty. We all know the temptation: the officer stops you, you are at fault, and someone slips in: “We can come to an arrangement.” A bill in the hand, and you drive off. It seems convenient at the moment, but when you pay “an arrangement”, you buy disobedience. You tell the country: the rule is for sale. And the rule for sale, one day, is what crushes you.

The responsible citizen does two things: he respects the rule so as not to get a fine, and if he receives one, he pays it through the official channel, and keeps the receipt. Respect also goes the other way: the user respects the law, the officer respects the user. If you are mistreated, there are remedies. Do not take justice into your own hands, and do not let yourself be intimidated either.

Pedestrians and passengers

Pedestrians: cross at the designated places, do not cross with your nose in your phone, do not play on the roadway. Passengers: you have a duty to speak. If the driver is driving like a madman, say: “Sir, slow down.” Keeping silent is becoming an accomplice.

One question to finish: when you are at the wheel or on your motorbike, who do you think of? If you think only of your appointment, you are a driver. If you think of the lives of others, you are a citizen.

The basic text is Law No. 98-004 of January 27, 1998 establishing the Labor Code. It is nearly thirty years old and has been supplemented by decrees, collective agreements and special texts, but it is still the backbone.

“Me, I have no contract: I work in small trade, crafts, the fields. This code is not for me.” You are partly right: a large part of employment is informal, and the Code applies concretely mainly to formal relationships. But even in the informal sector, the great principles hold: you must not be made to work without being paid, you must not be mistreated, children must not be made to work in forbidden conditions. And if you yourself are the boss of a workshop, a hair salon or a shop with employees, this code concerns you directly. If you understand your rights and duties well, you avoid half of the conflicts before they are born.

The contract: putting things in writing

The Code provides for the open-ended contract (CDI), the normal form of work; the fixed-term contract (CDD), for work limited in time; temporary work; internships and apprenticeship. A CDD of more than one month must be in writing, it cannot exceed two years and can be renewed only once.

My advice, even when the law does not require it: put everything in writing. The position, the salary, the hours, the duration. Not out of lack of trust, but because words fly away and writing remains.

Mariam is a seamstress. She hires Rose to help her: “I will pay you 30,000 a month, you arrive at eight o’clock, you leave at five.” Three months later, orders explode, Rose works until eight in the evening, and Mariam tells her: “But I paid you the same this month.”

If it is written, you can discuss calmly. If it is not written, you quarrel, and both lose. (Invented story.)

The minimum wage

The SMIG (guaranteed interprofessional minimum wage) is 52,000 CFA francs per month, since January 1, 2023, compared with 40,000 francs before. A private sector employer cannot pay a full-time employee less than this floor, under penalty of a fine. It is a floor, not an ideal: many deserve more, and some collective agreements (in banks, for example) provide higher scales. But no one has the right to go below it. Check the amount in force: it may be revalued by decree.

Working hours, rest, leave

  • The legal duration is 40 hours per week (outside the agricultural sector). Beyond that, these are overtime hours, which must be paid better. Sundays and holidays are paid at a higher rate. Every worker has the right to one weekly day of rest.
  • Paid leave: the employee earns two working days of leave per month of service, that is 24 days a year. It is not a favor from the boss, it is a right.
  • Maternity: the pregnant employee has the right to 14 weeks of maternity leave (generally six before and eight after the birth), with her salary. A mother must never be dismissed because she has become a mom: it is discrimination, and the law protects the employee during this leave.

Many of our fellow citizens agree to work sixty or seventy hours without being paid a franc more: “At least I have a job.” We understand the fear of unemployment, but it is not a gift: it is an injustice that we normalize. And to employers: a rested person works better. Wearing out your employees is not saving money, it is digging a hole.

What the employee also owes

Work is an exchange, and a responsible citizen does not look only at his rights. The employee must arrive on time, do the work he is paid for, be honest, not waste equipment, keep professional secrecy and respect his colleagues. Arriving late three times a week, using the office phone for one’s personal business, “borrowing” a little merchandise: you can call it what you want, it is theft, even small. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men” (Col 3:23). Working seriously when the boss is not looking is a form of worship.

What the employer also owes

  • Pay the salary on time. The apostle James says that the wages withheld from workers cry out to God (James 5:4). Delaying a salary is playing with someone’s rent, food and children’s school.
  • Ensure safe and healthy working conditions. Bare electrical wires, a construction site without helmets, a shop without an emergency exit: this is not only imprudent, it is forbidden.
  • Declare your employees to the CNSS (National Social Security Fund), which guarantees retirement, family allowances and coverage of work accidents. An undeclared employee is an employee without a safety net.
  • Provide a payslip that details the salary, the deductions and what the employee actually receives.
  • Respect the dignity of people. No slaps, no insults, no sexual harassment. Some employees, especially young ones, are given to understand that they will keep their job if they “make a gesture”: this is called sexual harassment. The Penal Code, supplemented in 2021, punishes it, and there are remedies.

When work stops

A contract can end by resignation, by dismissal or at the end of a CDD. A dismissal must have a real and serious reason: you do not dismiss in a fit of anger, because the employee fell ill or because he claimed his right. There is a notice period, the minimum length of which is fifteen days for hourly-paid workers, one month for monthly-paid workers, three months for supervisors and managers. During the notice period, the employee has free hours to look for a new job. In case of non-compliance, compensation is due.

Paul has worked for six years in a transport company. One Monday morning, his boss tells him: “You leave today, I no longer need you.” No letter, no notice, no explanation.

Paul does not have to leave in silence. He can go to the labor inspectorate, which first tries to conciliate. If conciliation fails, he can bring the matter before the labor court. (Invented story.)

A piece of advice for employees as for bosses: the first step in a conflict is neither threat, nor insult, nor fight. It is the labor inspector, a person paid by the State for that.

Children at work

The Code forbids employing a child before the age of 14, and certain dangerous work is forbidden to young people. Benin has also signed international conventions on the worst forms of child labor. Yet we see children selling at the roadside at the hour they should be in class, little girls carrying loads that are too heavy, boys in quarries. This is not right. We come back to it in part 8.

lecons.titre: The Code of Persons and the Family
lecons.html:
The text is Law No. 2002-07 of August 24, 2004 establishing the Code of Persons and the Family, amended and supplemented since. Before it, people lived with a mixture of customary law and texts inherited from the colonial period. This code wanted to set common rules, with principles of equality and freedom. A responsible citizen knows at least six points of it.

1. Marriage: it is not only a party

The Code recognizes only monogamous marriage. For it to be valid, the consent of both persons, of different sexes, is required. No one can force someone to marry: neither parents, nor family, nor custom. Forced marriage is forbidden.

This concerns us directly, we Christians. According to article 126, only the marriage celebrated by the civil registrar has legal effects. The mayor and his deputies perform this function. In other words, we begin with the town hall, and then we can bless the union at church. “But we got married at church.” That is beautiful. But before the law, without a civil marriage, you are not spouses. This poses very concrete problems: inheritance, the widow’s pension, the children’s papers, social security. Do both: the town hall and the church. It is not a betrayal of faith, it is wisdom.

Before marriage, the law asks for papers, including a birth certificate and a premarital certificate (medical tests). It is not to complicate things: it is so that each knows what he is getting into. The dowry has a symbolic character.

2. The age of marriage

Eighteen years, for girls as for boys. Not sixteen, not seventeen. Yet, according to child protection organizations, about three girls in ten under eighteen are still married or placed in union in Benin, and in some regions, far more. These are figures that should hurt us: a fourteen- or fifteen-year-old girl who is married off is a child withdrawn from school, who will carry a pregnancy too early with real risks to her health and the baby’s.

What should a parent do? Resist the pressure: if an uncle or a neighbor says “she is big now, she must be given away”, answer that the law and reason say no. What should a young man do? Not take advantage of a very young girl. What should a community do? Speak, protect, report.

3. Shared parental authority

Parental authority is the power and the duty of parents over their minor children: feeding them, caring for them, educating them, protecting them. During the marriage, it is exercised jointly by the father and the mother. Parents who endanger their child’s health, safety or morality can be stripped of it, in whole or in part. Being a parent is not a property right over the child: it is a responsibility. “Don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Eph 6:4). Raising is not crushing.

4. The birth certificate: the gateway to everything

A child without a birth certificate does not exist, legally. No easy school enrollment, no taking exams, no ID card later, no passport, no regular marriage, no simple access to an inheritance. Studies have shown that a significant number of children are not registered at birth.

The declaration is made to the civil registrar of the municipality, within the period provided by law: inquire at the town hall. After that period, a court judgment is needed to obtain a certificate (the substitute judgment), which is longer, more complicated and more costly. Do it right away, for your child, for your sister’s son, for the little girl you are housing.

5. Equality of children and inheritance

The Code establishes the equality of children in succession: boys and girls inherit from their father and mother, without distinction. This is not what certain old customary practices provided, where girls were set aside. The law also protects the status of the widow. We still see situations where, at the husband’s death, the family comes and takes everything (the land, the house, sometimes the children) and leaves the widow with nothing. This is not only unjust: it is contrary to the law.

Practical consequence: make a will if you have property, or at least speak clearly to your family. This avoids succession wars that destroy families for generations.

6. The duty of maintenance

Parents must feed, house, care for and school their children. This duty does not disappear when the couple separates. The law allows setting child support and punishes family abandonment. “She left, so I no longer pay anything”: this is false morally and legally. The child did not choose to leave the home. He keeps his right to be fed and cared for.

Law No. 2015-08 of December 8, 2015 establishes the Child Code. It takes up a large part of the international Convention on the Rights of the Child, which Benin ratified as early as 1990.

Who is a child?

According to article 2, a child is every human being under the age of eighteen. A seventeen-year-old, even tall, even if he works or owns a latest-model phone, remains a child before the law, and has the right to the Code’s protection. The text sets a principle that comes back everywhere: the best interests of the child. When a decision touches a child, whether it comes from a judge, a parent, a school principal or a village chief, the first question must be: what is best for this child?

Corporal punishment

The Code asks parents to apply family discipline with humanity and respect for the child’s dignity (art. 39), without harm to his physical integrity or cruel or degrading treatment. Corporal punishment is forbidden at school and in care facilities (art. 119), and the State must ensure that it is not practiced in the family, at school or in institutions (art. 130).

“Me, I was beaten, and look, I became somebody.” Many of us grew up like that. But having succeeded despite the blows does not prove that the blows helped: many succeed thanks to a loving grandmother, a good teacher, their own courage. There is a difference between correcting and hurting. Correcting is explaining, setting limits, removing a privilege, having what was broken repaired. Hurting is hitting with a cord, a stick, a belt, and leaving marks. A child who is hit learns that the stronger is right. A child to whom things are explained learns that the rule has a reason. “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” (Prov 22:6) The word is train. Not break.

Protecting the child against exploitation

The Code protects the child against every form of exploitation and violence (art. 129): torture, the sale of children, sexual exploitation, forced begging, economic exploitation, and harmful practices such as early marriage, forced marriage and female genital mutilation.

The placed child (the “vidomègon”)

The Code defines the placed child, or vidomègon, as a child who lives outside his family of origin and who is placed with a third family (art. 3). Placing a child with a relative or an acquaintance, so that he studies or learns a trade, is an old practice. In itself, it is not bad: many great men and women grew up at an uncle’s or an aunt’s.

The problem begins when the placed child becomes free labor: he gets up at five to fetch water, sweep, cook, sell at the market, while the other children of the house sleep and then go to school. He is deprived of schooling, he is hit, he is not cared for. Here, it is exploitation, and the law protects this child: any corporal punishment or any form of violence is forbidden toward him (art. 220), and the Code provides for his follow-up and schooling (art. 217 to 221).

Ask yourself these questions at home. Is there a child who is not mine? Is he treated like the others? Does he go to school? Does he eat at the same table? Does he sleep in a real bed? If the answer is no, it is time to correct it.

The duties of the child, school and health

The Code does not speak only of rights. The child also has responsibilities according to his age: respecting his parents and elderly people, studying, taking part in family life, not harming others. Rights without duties produce spoiled children. Duties without rights produce submissive children. Both are needed.

Finally, school. The Constitution says that primary education is compulsory (art. 13). A parent who keeps a child at home to sell or to watch the little ones deprives that child of his future. The child also has the right to health: vaccines, consultations, care. A sick child treated only with herbal teas when a doctor is needed is a risk taken with his life.

Knowing the law is good. Knowing what to do when an authority shows up in front of you is better. Here are six situations. In each: stay calm, stay respectful, and know your rights.

The situationWhat you can doWhat you must doThe common mistake
Identity check in the streetPolitely ask the reason for the check. If you are asked to unlock your phone, ask on what legal basis (your communications are protected, art. 21) and call a lawyer.Show your ID. Stay calm and respectful. Do not flee, do not resist.Insulting the officer, refusing to identify yourself, or trying to bribe.
Search at homeAsk to see the written order of the judicial authority (warrant). Your home is inviolable (art. 20). Stay present and have a witness.Stay calm. Let them work if the order is regular. Note everything that is seized.Letting officers in without a written order. Signing a report without reading it entirely.
Arrest following a publication (OCRC)Ask the exact nature of the accusation. Ask for a lawyer right away. Notify your family.Stay calm. Sign nothing before having read and understood, preferably in the presence of your lawyer.Explaining yourself alone to the officers, wanting to justify your publication. Signing a confession under pressure.
Police custodyRemind them of the 48-hour limit without a magistrate’s decision (art. 18). Ask to be examined by a doctor of your choice. Your defense is guaranteed (art. 17).Stay calm, give your identity, and have your requests noted.Staying silent for days without asking for a lawyer or contact with family.
A neighbor’s noise complaintAsk for the noise to be measured. If you are within the norms, you are protected.Obtain the opinion of the Departmental Directorate of the Living Environment. Respect the hours. Soundproof if necessary.Ignoring an official summons. Negotiating amicably without settling the legal situation.
Traffic stop and “arrangement”Ask for the official ticket and pay it through the official channel, with a receipt.Present the vehicle papers and the license. Stay courteous.Offering or agreeing to pay “to make an arrangement”.

Your right to a lawyer and to a fair trial comes from the Constitution (art. 17) and the African Charter (art. 7). Keep these references in mind, and keep a lawyer’s number.

lecons.titre: Conclusion: the law is for us
lecons.html:
We have gone through nine texts. Remember a few simple ideas.

  • The law is not against us, it is for us. The road is made so that we come home alive. The Labor Code is made so that work does not become slavery. The Family Code and the Child Code are made so that the home is a place of safety.
  • You have rights: worship, assembly, defense, home, communications. Rely on them calmly.
  • You have limits: what you say, what you publish, the noise you make.
  • You have duties: taxes, respect for the laws, for public property, for your family.
  • Laws change. Read the texts in force, and ask a professional for advice when it is serious.

“For rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil” (Rom 13:3), and we must be in subjection “also for conscience’ sake” (Rom 13:5). The goal of this module is not to make you fear the law. It is to make you citizens who respect it by conviction, who know what it says, and who also know what it guarantees them.

It is said that a country’s road is built with tar. It is built first with habits. Every time you put on the helmet, pay the salary on time, register the child with civil registration, send a girl to school rather than to marriage, you lay a stone. A single stone does not make a country. But thousands of stones laid by thousands of hands do.

The challenge of the week. Choose just one thing from everything you have read: the helmet for the passenger, the written contract with your employee, the birth certificate of the youngest, the civil marriage, checking a message before forwarding it, the opinion of the Living Environment directorate for your place of worship. And do it before Sunday.

objectifs: ✦  You know your fundamental rights (Constitution, African Charter) and you know where to read them.
✦  You know what the law allows and forbids to someone who preaches, teaches or leads an assembly.
✦  You know the common offenses on social networks and you no longer commit them.
✦  You know how to organize a place of worship in compliance with the noise regulation.
✦  You know the basic rules of the road, of work, of the family and of the child.
✦  You know how to react when facing an authority: identity check, search, arrest, a neighbor’s complaint.
✦  You respect the law by conviction, not out of fear.

qcm.q: According to Romans 13, why does the Christian submit to authorities and to the law?
c: Only out of fear of punishment
For conscience’s sake: authority is instituted by God, and we respect it by conviction, not only out of fear
Because the Christian has no right to assert
Because laws are always perfect
qcm.e: Romans 13:5: “not only because of the wrath, but also for conscience’ sake”. Obeying is not keeping silent: it is knowing the law, respecting it and knowing how to have it respected when it protects us.

qcm.q: An officer has held you for three days without any magistrate’s decision. Which rule of the Constitution do you calmly recall?
c: Art. 33: the duty to pay taxes
Art. 18: no one may be held more than 48 hours without the decision of a magistrate
Art. 26: equality before the law, which authorizes any length of custody
Art. 37: the protection of public property
qcm.e: Beyond 48 hours, a magistrate’s decision is needed. Extension is possible only in exceptional cases provided for by law, and never beyond eight days. You can also ask to be examined by a doctor of your choice.

qcm.q: Why do we say that “the pulpit is not a courtroom”?
c: Because the pulpit is forbidden to criticisms of any public policy
Because only magistrates have the right to preach
Because publicly accusing a named person, without established proof, exposes you to article 388 of the Penal Code; there are provided channels: letter, complaint, lawyer
Because a leader has no right to speak of justice
qcm.e: You can criticize a situation or a decision. What the law punishes is the accusation of a person, by name, of a specific act, without proof. The pulpit is for teaching, exhorting and praying, not for settling scores.

qcm.q: Among these actions by an assembly leader, which remains permitted?
c: Calling to refuse to pay a certain tax
Opposing the officers of the State
Praying for leaders and encouraging worshipers to vote, to inform themselves and to go through legal channels
Telling the assembly not to obey a certain law
qcm.e: The line runs between teaching and praying (permitted) on one side, and pushing people to resist or setting citizens against one another (article 389: three months to two years in prison) on the other. The apostles of Acts 5 answer for their own acts: they do not rouse the crowd.

qcm.q: A friend sends you false information about a politician and you share it in your WhatsApp group. What does the module say?
c: You may be concerned by article 550 of the Digital Code, which also targets the one who relays; before forwarding, you must verify the source
Only the first one who published is prosecuted
You are not concerned: you are not the author
A WhatsApp group is a private space that the law never touches
qcm.e: Article 550 targets whoever initiates or relays false information. Saying “it is my friend who sent it to me” does not automatically protect you: the judge assesses. The rule: before forwarding, verify. If you cannot verify, do not share.

qcm.q: Why does a closed WhatsApp group not shelter you?
c: Because only groups of more than 100 people are protected
Because WhatsApp automatically passes all messages to the police
Because messages can be captured, forwarded and used as proof
Because the law forbids WhatsApp groups
qcm.e: Even in private or in a closed group, the digital proof remains. What you publish online is judged like what a newspaper publishes on paper (article 558).

qcm.q: According to Decree No. 2022-301, when are noisy activities, including in places of worship, forbidden in residential areas, on a working day?
c: Only from midnight to 4 a.m.
From 1 p.m. to 3 p.m. and from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.
Never: the decree speaks only of bars and parties
From 6 p.m. to 8 p.m.
qcm.e: On rest days, the ban runs from 8 p.m. to 10 a.m. The text targets the noise that goes out from your place, not the fact of gathering to pray.

qcm.q: For an exceptional event (convention, large vigil), what does the decree on noise provide?
c: No step is necessary for a place of worship
A one-week exemption granted by a simple call to the neighbor
A permanent authorization granted once and for all
An exemption from the mayor, on a written request made beforehand, limited to 80 decibels and 48 hours
qcm.e: The authorization specifies the date, place and duration. Without a prior request, a convention with sound equipment remains exposed to a complaint, to the officers’ findings and to seizure of equipment.

qcm.q: An officer stops you for a driving offense and slips in: “We can come to an arrangement.” What does the responsible citizen do?
c: He refuses the “arrangement”, asks for the official ticket, pays it through the official channel and keeps the receipt
He haggles to get a discount
He slips in a bill to save time
He runs away to avoid the check
qcm.e: Paying an “arrangement” is buying disobedience and saying the rule is for sale. The user respects the law, the officer respects the user: if you are mistreated, there are remedies.

qcm.q: An employer dismisses Paul, after six years of work, overnight, with no letter, no notice and no explanation. What can Paul do?
c: Publish accusations on Facebook
Go to the labor inspectorate, which first tries to conciliate; if it fails, he can bring the matter before the labor court
Threaten his boss or fight him
Leave in silence: he has no recourse
qcm.e: A dismissal must have a real and serious reason and respect a notice period. In case of conflict, the first step is neither threat nor insult: it is the labor inspector.

qcm.q: A couple married only at church. What is their situation before the law?
c: They are married if the dowry was paid
They are fully married: the church has the same legal effect as the town hall
Without a civil marriage before the civil registrar, they are not legally married (art. 126), which creates problems for inheritance, the widow’s pension and the children’s papers
They are married if two witnesses affirm it
qcm.e: Only the marriage celebrated by the civil registrar has legal effects. We begin with the town hall, then we can bless the union at church: it is not a betrayal of faith, it is wisdom.

qcm.q: A family wants to marry off their 16-year-old daughter to a neighbor: “she is big now, she must be given away”. What does the module say?
c: At sixteen, with the parents’ consent, it is permitted
Only the Church decides the age of marriage
The law forbids nothing as long as the party is held
The legal age of marriage is eighteen, for girls as for boys: the parent must resist the pressure
qcm.e: A fourteen- or fifteen-year-old girl who is married off is a child withdrawn from school, with real risks to her health.

qcm.q: Why must you register your child with civil registration from birth?
c: Without a birth certificate, the child does not legally exist: school, exams, ID card, passport, marriage and inheritance become difficult
It is useful only in adulthood
To pay fewer taxes
Only to give him a family name
qcm.e: After the period provided by law, a court judgment (substitute judgment) is needed, which is longer and more costly.

qcm.q: According to the module, when does a child placed with a relative or acquaintance (the “vidomègon”) become a problem?
c: As soon as he studies or learns a trade
As soon as he lives in a family other than his own
When he receives gifts from the host family
When he becomes free labor: deprived of schooling, hit, not cared for, treated differently from the other children
qcm.e: Placing a child so that he studies or learns a trade is an old practice, not bad in itself. When it becomes exploitation, the law protects the child: any corporal punishment or violence is forbidden toward him (art. 220), and the Code provides for his follow-up and schooling.

qcm.q: A father wants to “correct” his son by hitting him with an electric cord. What does the Child Code say?
c: Discipline must be done with humanity, without harm to physical integrity or cruel treatment: correcting is explaining and setting limits
The law does not deal with what happens in the family
Everything is permitted when the father is a Christian
Blows are permitted at home if they leave no marks
qcm.e: Article 39: respect for the child’s dignity. Having succeeded despite the blows does not prove that the blows helped.

exercices.consigne: Answer the 12 statements. After each choice, you see the expected answer with a short explanation. It is not graded: it is to help you remember.

champs.label: 1. Sharing false information on WhatsApp exposes me to article 550 of the Digital Code, even if I am not its author.
champs.explication: The article speaks of the one who initiates or who relays.

champs.label: 2. A private WhatsApp group is not concerned by the Digital Code.
champs.explication: A closed group does not shelter you: messages are forwarded, captured and used as proof.

champs.label: 3. Criticizing a minister’s decision on Facebook is forbidden by law.
champs.explication: Criticizing a decision is permitted, with facts and a proper tone. What poses a problem is insult or accusation without proof against the person.

champs.label: 4. Insulting someone because of his religion in a Facebook comment can lead to up to seven years in prison.
champs.explication: Seven years is the maximum provided in article 551 of the Digital Code.

champs.label: 5. A soundproofed place of worship can make as much noise as it wants inside.
champs.explication: The ceiling is 70 decibels, even in a soundproofed building.

champs.label: 6. Decree 2022-301 forbids religious meetings after 10 p.m. on working days.
champs.explication: False, with a nuance: the decree forbids noise at those hours in residential areas, not the meeting itself. But if your meeting makes noise that goes outside, you are in violation.

champs.label: 7. An officer can hold me more than 48 hours in police custody without a magistrate’s decision.
champs.explication: Beyond 48 hours, a magistrate’s decision is needed, and extension is possible only in exceptional cases provided for by law (Constitution, art. 18).

champs.label: 8. A public criticism of a civil servant cited by name in a sermon can fall under article 388 of the Penal Code.
champs.explication: Publicly accusing a named person, without proof, can constitute defamation.

champs.label: 9. A marriage celebrated only at church has full legal effects.
champs.explication: Only the marriage celebrated by the civil registrar has legal effects (Code of Persons and the Family, art. 126).

champs.label: 10. A seventeen-year-old is a child before the law.
champs.explication: A child is every human being under eighteen (Child Code, art. 2).

champs.label: 11. An employer can pay a full-time employee less than the SMIG if both agree.
champs.explication: The SMIG is a floor: no agreement can go below it.

champs.label: 12. The helmet is mandatory for the motorcycle driver, but not for the passenger.
champs.explication: Wearing a helmet is mandatory for the driver and for the passenger.

exercices.consigne: Three situations taken from the part on fundamental rights, then a little research to do on the spot. Reread the lesson “Your fundamental rights” if needed.

champs.label: Someone tries to ban a prayer meeting in your neighborhood. What do you rely on, calmly?
options: Freedom of religion and worship (art. 23) and freedom of assembly (art. 25), with the African Charter (art. 8, 10 and 11)
The duty to protect public property (art. 37)
No text: you must obey without discussion
champs.bonne: Freedom of religion and worship (art. 23) and freedom of assembly (art. 25), with the African Charter (art. 8, 10 and 11)
champs.explication: These are not favors, they are rights. They are exercised with respect for public order: you rely on them calmly, without insulting or opposing the officers.

champs.label: An officer has held you for three days without charge. Which article do you invoke?
options: Art. 18: no more than 48 hours without a magistrate’s decision
Art. 33: the duty to pay taxes
Art. 36: the duty to respect one’s fellow man
Art. 37: the protection of public property
champs.bonne: Art. 18: no more than 48 hours without a magistrate’s decision
champs.explication: You can also recall your guaranteed defense (art. 17) and ask to be examined by a doctor of your choice. Stay calm and have your requests noted.

champs.label: An officer shows up at your home to search the house. What do you do before opening?
options: Nothing: an agent of the State can enter anywhere
I ask him to show me the written order of the judicial authority, because my home is inviolable (art. 20)
I let him in to avoid trouble, then I sign what he gives me
I close the door and hide my things
champs.bonne: I ask him to show me the written order of the judicial authority, because my home is inviolable (art. 20)
champs.explication: Stay calm, keep a witness with you, let them work if the order is regular and note everything that is seized. Never sign a report without reading it entirely.

champs.label: Research: what steps are needed to legally register a religious association? Find out (town hall, prefecture, your Church’s leader) and note what you found. If you do not have the answer yet, write what you know and whom you will ask.

exercices.titre: Before publishing: do I publish or not?
exercices.consigne: Five invented situations. For each, decide whether you publish or not, then look at the explanation.
exercices.intro_html:
The four questions before publishing: (1) Am I calling someone to disobey a law? (2) Am I naming a person, and do I have what it takes to prove it? (3) Would I dare say exactly the same thing to this person, to their face, in front of a witness? (4) Does this build something, or does it mainly relieve me?

If even one of these answers bothers you, do not publish tonight. Sleep on it, and reread your text tomorrow.

champs.label: Message received from a friend: “Urgent, share before it gets deleted: the director of the city hospital embezzled the money for medicines!” You have no proof.
options: I do not publish, I do not forward
champs.bonne: I do not publish, I do not forward
champs.explication: Relaying false information can fall under article 550. Who is the source? Is the information found in a serious media outlet? If you cannot verify, you do not share. “Share before it gets deleted” messages are precisely the ones you must not relay.

champs.label: A very funny video is circulating: it makes fun of the followers of another religion. Your friends laugh and forward it.
options: I do not publish, I do not forward
I publish, it is just a joke
champs.bonne: I do not publish, I do not forward
champs.explication: Mockery of a person because of his faith can fall under article 551 (six months to seven years in prison), even as a joke. You can explain why you believe something else “with humility and fear” (1 Pet 3:15), without lowering a person.

champs.label: You want to publish: “The waste management in our municipality does not meet the needs of the inhabitants. Here are three photos and the town hall’s figures. Let us pray and act together so that it changes.”
options: I do not publish, it is forbidden to criticize
champs.explication: Here, you are speaking of a situation and a decision, with facts and a proper tone. A criticism that rests on facts is easily defended before a judge.

champs.label: A preacher wants to write on Facebook: “Brothers and sisters, stop paying this tax, it is unjust. Tell your neighbors.”
options: He publishes: he trusts his conscience
champs.explication: Calling to refuse a tax is calling to disobey the law: articles 389 and 391 of the Penal Code, and a published writing counts as much as a word. You can go through legal channels: letter to the town hall, association, petition, lawyer.

champs.label: You want to publish: “Mr. So-and-so, of the technical department, stole the municipality’s money.” You are sure, but you have no proof.
options: I do not publish, I go through the provided channels (letter, complaint, lawyer)
I publish: the truth must be known
champs.bonne: I do not publish, I go through the provided channels (letter, complaint, lawyer)
champs.explication: Accusing a named person of a specific act, without proof, is exactly what the law punishes (defamation, article 558 online). Even if you think you are right: the pulpit, like Facebook, is not a courtroom.

champs.label: I reread the four questions before publishing and I keep them in mind: am I calling people to disobey? am I naming someone without proof? would I dare say it to their face in front of a witness? does this build?

exercices.titre: Noise and my place of worship
exercices.consigne: Five cases: compliant or violation? Then apply the decree to your own situation. Reread the lesson “The decree on noise” if needed.

champs.label: A prayer vigil with sound equipment, on a Tuesday from 9 p.m. to 11:30 p.m., in a residential neighborhood.
champs.explication: On working days, noise is forbidden from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. (and from 1 p.m. to 3 p.m.) in residential areas, places of worship included.

champs.label: A Sunday service that starts at 7 a.m. with drums and amplifiers, audible in the street.
champs.explication: On rest days, noise is forbidden from 8 p.m. to 10 a.m.

champs.label: Street evangelism with a loudspeaker, on a Tuesday at 4 p.m.
champs.explication: Outdoor sound devices (loudspeakers, sirens, horns) are forbidden, except to report an accident or serious incident.

champs.label: A three-day convention (72 hours), with outdoor sound equipment, relying on an exemption from the mayor.
champs.explication: An exceptional exemption is limited to 80 decibels and 48 hours at most, and is requested in writing beforehand.

champs.label: A Sunday service at 11 a.m., loudspeakers facing inward, nothing audible in the street, and the place of worship has the opinion of the Departmental Directorate of the Living Environment.
champs.explication: The text targets the noise that goes out from your place, not the fact of gathering to pray. The officers can measure the noise: if you are within the norms, you are protected.

champs.label: My situation
options: I lead a place of worship

exercices.titre: Real situations: what do you do?
exercices.consigne: For each of these six situations, choose the right reaction. After each choice, you see the expected reaction and the common mistake to avoid.

champs.label: Identity check in the street: the officer asks for your ID, then to unlock your phone.
options: I refuse to identify myself: I have nothing to hide
I show my ID, I stay calm, I politely ask the reason, and for the phone I ask on what legal basis (my communications are protected, art. 21) while asking for a lawyer
I walk away quickly to avoid trouble
I slip a bill so it ends quickly
champs.bonne: I show my ID, I stay calm, I politely ask the reason, and for the phone I ask on what legal basis (my communications are protected, art. 21) while asking for a lawyer
champs.explication: You show your ID, you stay calm and respectful, you do not flee and you do not resist. The common mistake: insulting the officer, refusing to identify yourself or trying to bribe.

champs.label: Officers show up at your home early in the morning and want to search the house.
options: I let them in without asking anything, to avoid trouble
I stay calm, I ask to see the written order of the judicial authority, I keep a witness with me and I note everything that is seized
I quickly sign their report so that they leave
champs.bonne: I stay calm, I ask to see the written order of the judicial authority, I keep a witness with me and I note everything that is seized
champs.explication: Your home is inviolable (art. 20). If the order is regular, you let them work. The common mistakes: letting them in without a written order, and signing a report without reading it entirely.

champs.label: You are arrested following one of your publications (OCRC).
options: I explain myself at length, alone, to justify my publication
I sign their documents so it goes quickly
I ask the exact nature of the accusation, a lawyer right away, I notify my family and I sign nothing before having read and understood
champs.bonne: I ask the exact nature of the accusation, a lawyer right away, I notify my family and I sign nothing before having read and understood
champs.explication: Stay calm. The common mistake: explaining yourself alone to the officers, wanting to justify your publication, or signing a confession under pressure.

champs.label: You are in police custody.
options: I stay silent for days without asking for anything
I recall the 48-hour limit without a magistrate’s decision (art. 18), I ask for a doctor of my choice, I recall my guaranteed defense (art. 17) and I have my requests noted, calmly
I confess everything to get out faster
I insult the officer to show that I am not guilty
champs.bonne: I recall the 48-hour limit without a magistrate’s decision (art. 18), I ask for a doctor of my choice, I recall my guaranteed defense (art. 17) and I have my requests noted, calmly
champs.explication: You give your identity, you stay calm and you have your requests noted. The common mistake: staying for days without asking for either a lawyer or contact with family.

champs.label: A neighbor files a complaint about your place of worship’s noise and you receive an official summons.
options: I ignore the summons: it will pass
I negotiate informally with the neighbor, without settling anything else
I ask for the noise to be measured, I answer the summons, and I settle the legal situation: opinion of the Departmental Directorate of the Living Environment, hours, soundproofing
I turn up the volume in protest
champs.bonne: I ask for the noise to be measured, I answer the summons, and I settle the legal situation: opinion of the Departmental Directorate of the Living Environment, hours, soundproofing
champs.explication: If you are within the norms, you are protected. The classic mistake: ignoring a summons or negotiating informally without settling the legal situation. And a courteous exchange with the neighbor is worth more than ten explanations before an officer (Rom 12:18).

champs.label: Traffic stop: you are at fault, and the officer slips in: “We can come to an arrangement.”
options: I ask for the official ticket, I pay it through the official channel and I keep the receipt
I offer money to settle quickly
I refuse to present my papers
champs.bonne: I ask for the official ticket, I pay it through the official channel and I keep the receipt
champs.explication: You present the vehicle papers and your license, you stay courteous. Offering or agreeing to pay “to make an arrangement” is buying disobedience.

exercices.titre: Reading the law at the source: 4 weeks
exercices.consigne: One reading mission per week, in the official text: this is the difference between someone who has heard about the law and someone who holds it in his hands. Each week, you tick “I read” and note what you retained. You can continue the course as soon as you have started.
exercices.intro_html: Texts change: always check the version in force. Official texts can be found notably from the National Assembly, the General Secretariat of the Government (sgg.gouv.bj) and, for the African Charter, from the African Union (au.int).

cibles: Week 1: the Constitution of Benin, articles 7 to 40 (rights and duties). Note the article most important for your daily life, a duty you were not fulfilling, and a right you were not aware of.
Week 2: the Digital Code, Book VI (cybercrime), articles 548 to 560. Note in one sentence what article 550 forbids, with two examples from your daily life.
Week 3: Decree No. 2022-301 on noise, in full (notably articles 7, 10, 14, 17 and 18). Note the points of non-compliance to correct, or what you will pass on to your leader.

Week 4: the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights, articles 1 to 18 (rights) and 27 to 29 (duties). Note how article 8 reinforces your freedom to practice your faith and which duties of article 29 concern you most.
